title: Judges 21:13–25
context: Israel makes peace with the six hundred Benjamites at the rock of Rimmon and gives them the women from Jabesh Gilead, but not enough. The elders then devise a scheme for the remaining men to seize young women dancing at the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, and to excuse it by arguing that the fathers had not technically broken the oath. The book ends with the refrain that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, echoing Deuteronomy 12:8 and the earlier frames at 17:6, 18:1 and 19:1. Interpreters commonly connect this refrain with the coming monarchy, though the books of Samuel and Kings show that human kings did not fully solve Israel’s problem. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly share this reading, and many in both traditions see the deepest answer in God’s own righteous King (compare Isaiah 9:7; Luke 1:32–33).

verses.text: The whole congregation sent and spoke to the children of Benjamin who were in the rock of Rimmon, and proclaimed peace to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the congregation proclaiming peace to the Benjamites at the rock of Rimmon. Reconciliation begins, though shaped by earlier violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peace offering as a step toward restoring the tribe. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a hopeful note in a dark context.

verses.text: Benjamin returned at that time; and they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh Gilead. There still weren’t enough for them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the women of Jabesh Gilead are given to Benjamin, but there are still not enough. The solution is incomplete and morally compromised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shortfall as leading to yet another troubling scheme. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as showing how human solutions apart from God fall short.

verses.text: The people grieved for Benjamin, because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the statement that the people grieved because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes. The narrator links the loss to God’s judgment while Israel’s own actions are evident.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as affirming God’s sovereign hand in judgment, even through human actions. Both traditions commonly hold together God’s sovereignty and human responsibility here without turning it into a dispute.

verses.text: Then the elders of the congregation said, “How shall we provide wives for those who remain, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the elders asking how to provide wives for the remaining Benjamites. Leadership is focused on preserving the tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the concern for the tribe’s survival as legitimate, even though the means chosen will be wrong. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the final scheme.

verses.text: They said, “There must be an inheritance for those who are escaped of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the elders’ desire that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel. The concern for covenant unity is real.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the commitment to preserving every tribe as reflecting God’s promises to Israel. Both traditions commonly see the goal as worthy, while the methods remain deeply troubling.

verses.text: However, we may not give them wives of our daughters, for the children of Israel had sworn, saying, ‘Cursed is he who gives a wife to Benjamin.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the elders bound by the oath not to give their daughters to Benjamin. The rash vow continues to drive their decisions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath as a snare of the people’s own making (compare Ecclesiastes 5:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as illustrating the danger of vows sworn in anger.

verses.text: They said, “Behold, there is a feast of the LORD from year to year in Shiloh, which is on the north of Bethel, on the east side of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the mention of a feast of the LORD at Shiloh, located by the text in relation to Bethel, Shechem and Lebonah. A sacred occasion becomes the setting for the scheme.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the misuse of a feast of the LORD as part of the narrative’s critique. Both traditions commonly observe that the precise identification of the feast is not stated and avoid speculating about it.

verses.text: They commanded the children of Benjamin, saying, “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the elders commanding the Benjamites to lie in wait in the vineyards. The plan relies on ambush rather than consent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the instruction as the elders sanctioning wrongdoing. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the moral collapse the narrator exposes.

verses.text: and see, and behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards, and each man catch his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the plan to seize the daughters of Shiloh as they come out to dance. The young women are given no voice or choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abduction as a grave wrong, presented by the narrator without approval. Both traditions commonly honor the dignity of these young women and read the verse as part of what the closing refrain judges.

verses.text: It shall be, when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, that we will say to them, ‘Grant them graciously to us, because we didn’t take for each man his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them; otherwise you would now be guilty.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the elders’ plan to persuade the fathers and brothers to accept the situation by appealing to technicalities about the oath. The scheme seeks to avoid guilt rather than to do right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see legal maneuvering here substituting for justice and repentance. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing how people can rationalize wrongdoing while claiming to keep their word.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin did so, and took wives for themselves according to their number, of those who danced, whom they carried off. They went and returned to their inheritance, built the cities, and lived in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Benjamites carrying out the plan, taking wives and returning to rebuild their cities. The tribe survives, but at a moral cost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the restoration of Benjamin as preserving the tribe through flawed human actions. Both traditions commonly note that Benjamin later produces Saul, the first king (compare 1 Samuel 10:26), without claiming the narrator intends a direct link.

verses.text: The children of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and to his family, and they each went out from there to his own inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Israelites return home, each to his tribe and family. The crisis ends, but the damage remains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the dispersal as closing the story without resolution of the deeper problems. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for the book’s final verdict.

verses.text: In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the closing refrain as the narrator’s verdict on the whole period: without faithful leadership, everyone did what was right in his own eyes (compare Deuteronomy 12:8). The book ends by exposing the need for righteous rule under God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the refrain as framing chapters 17–21, and interpreters commonly connect it with the monarchy that follows in Samuel. Many in both traditions see the deepest answer not in any human king but in God’s righteous King (compare Isaiah 9:7; Luke 1:32–33).
